question: What disaster does Joel describe, and what groups of people does he call to weep or mourn?
Verse 4 uses four names for locusts, among them אַרְבֶּה (’arbeh): what does the sequence of waves of insects convey about the scale of the plague?
Why does the lack of offerings in the house of the LORD worry the prophet so much, and how is the plague linked to the announcement of the “day of the LORD”?
Joel asks that what happened be told to the children and grandchildren: what hard experiences of your story are worth passing on, and for what purpose?
How is the army that comes on the day of the LORD described, and what effects does it cause on earth and in the sky?
The verb שׁוּב (shuv, “return”) appears in the invitation “return to Me” and in the question “who knows? He may turn and relent”: how does the text set the people's return and God's side by side?
What changes does the LORD promise after the people gather to cry out, and how do they answer the losses described in chapter 1?
Who receives the Spirit in verses 28 and 29, and what is new in this list of people?
“Rend your hearts and not your garments”: what difference do you see between a repentance that is only outward and one from within?
Of what does the LORD accuse the nations, and Tyre, Sidon and Philistia in particular, in the judgment in the Valley of Jehoshaphat?
The name Jehoshaphat means “the LORD judges,” and the verb שָׁפַט (shafat, “judge”) appears with it: what relationship does the text establish between the place and what happens there?
Verse 10 reverses a well-known image from Isaiah and Micah, of swords turned into plowshares: what does this reversal suggest about the moment described here?
The LORD is called “a refuge for His people” while heaven and earth tremble: in what shaking situation do you need to remember this image?
